how.heading: Three steps, and the rule that ends each one

compare.heading: Against the other two ways to fill this

steps.title: Read the page
steps.body: Analytics, session recordings, support tickets, and whatever sales gets asked twice a week. Most of what you need is usually already inside the company before anyone runs anything.

steps.title: Write it down before running it
steps.body: Hypothesis, metric, sample size, duration, stopping rule. All of it agreed before the variant gets built, so that when the result comes in there is nothing left to argue about except what to do next.

steps.title: Turn the result into a brief
steps.body: Most tests lose. Kohavi's published base rate is roughly one in three ideas improving its target metric. So the write-up matters more than the result: a loss you can explain still changes what gets built next, and plenty of wins can't be explained at all.

projects.title: PDP redesign: Candles 4 The Culture
projects.blurb: Product page concept for a culture-inspired candle brand.
projects.alt: Candles 4 The Culture product page on a phone, live version beside the redesign
projects.caption: before / after, mobile

modal.situation: Candles 4 The Culture hand-pours culture-inspired candles in Atlanta. Its $20 Bebe's Kids candle sells a "nostalgic cereal scent" on a near-stock Shopify theme with one product photo. Unsolicited, with no client and no traffic access.
modal.found: 7 of 10 reviews compare it to a cereal, but the page never names one. There is no gift option before checkout, "Free shipping for U.S. orders $75 and up" appears only on the policy page, and on mobile a doubled cookie banner covers the screen under the price.
modal.hypothesis: Leading the buy box with "Smells like a bowl of fruity cereal in front of Saturday-morning cartoons.", a customer quote and liner notes from the jar label will raise add-to-cart rate.
modal.result: Not run: no traffic access. Pre-registered instead, on assumed baselines: 9,907 visitors per arm for add-to-cart rate (7.0% to 8.05%), 21,750 for orders with a gift note (5% to 10%), and 78,250 for orders of $75 or more (15% to 18.75%).
modal.changed: A rebuilt product page with the scent in words, a free gift note and a cart drawer, the $75 free-shipping line and a solid button. Plus a Saturday-morning landing variant: "Your Saturday mornings, in a jar."

projects.title: Homepage redesign: Free To Eat
projects.blurb: Homepage concept for an allergen-free cookie brand.
projects.alt: Free To Eat homepage on a phone, live version beside the redesign
projects.caption: before / after, mobile

modal.situation: Free To Eat bakes allergen-free cookies in its own bakery in Loveland, Colorado, a claim no competitor I checked makes. Its homepage opens on a snack-pack launch notice. Unsolicited, with no client and no traffic access.
modal.found: The first screen fails a 5-second test: "TOP 9 ALLERGEN FREE" appears only on the pack in the photo. The certifications are one logo image about 75% down, the allergen claim is worded four ways across the site, and mobile LCP is 12.7s.
modal.hypothesis: Replacing the launch hero with "A real, soft cookie.", a live-text top 9 line and a "Shop soft-baked cookies" button will send more homepage visitors to a product page.
modal.result: Not run: no traffic access. Pre-registered instead, on assumed baselines: 3,763 visitors per arm for homepage-to-PDP click-through (30% to 33%), 36,693 for homepage-session CVR (2.0% to 2.3%), and 25,740 for add-to-cart rate (6.0% to 6.6%).
modal.changed: A rebuilt homepage with a promise hero, a live-text proof band and three credited taste reviews, one offer instead of four, and mobile LCP down from 14.7s to 1.7s in a local stand-in test (not Lighthouse). Plus a gluten-free hero variant: "Gluten-free. You'd never know."

projects.title: PDP redesign: Northbound Gear Adventure Pants
projects.blurb: Unsolicited concept. Why buyers pick the wrong size and miss the 2nd-pair offer, a rebuilt page around three hypotheses, and one ad-audience variant.
projects.alt: Northbound Gear product page on a phone, live version beside the redesign
projects.caption: before / after, mobile

modal.situation: Northbound Gear's Adventure Pants page has 4.9 stars from 1,508 reviews, but on a phone the price and Add to cart sit 1,250px down. Unsolicited, with no client and no traffic access: what was at stake was a sizing problem visible in the brand's own reviews.
modal.found: The page says the fit is true to size and to size up for comfort, while 8 of 64 reviews I coded say the calf is slim and two sized up into a loose waist. The 2nd-pair 40% offer, relevant to the 14 of 64 reviewers who own two or more pairs, is two paragraphs of prose and disappears in the cart.
modal.hypothesis: Putting "Waist runs true to size." and a Size & fit guide that opens on the tapered leg at the waist picker will raise net kept orders per visitor and lower size-related returns.
modal.result: Not run: no traffic access. Pre-registered instead: 53,541 visitors per arm for net kept orders (1.38% to 1.59%) and 2,554 orders per arm for size returns (8% to 6%), read about 12 weeks after the last order.
modal.changed: A rebuilt page with three tagged changes (price first, fit at the picker, a visible 2nd-pair offer), plus a worker-audience variant built from the most-voted review.

faq.question: Have you done this for a real client?
faq.answer: I'm switching over from a career in Computer Science, so the work here is self-initiated. The methods are the same as what I would use for a client.

faq.question: You're applying for two different jobs.
faq.answer: I'm open to various roles as I would love to get a step into the industry. I have a strong interest in both creative and web strategy, and I believe my skills can be valuable in either area.

faq.question: How many tests have you actually run?
faq.answer: Not many yet. Running a real test needs a brand's traffic, so both case studies here are pre-registered with the sample size each test would need.
